title: Upon some verses of Virgil
paragraphs: The more profitable our thoughts are — the fuller and more solid — the more cumbersome and heavy they also become: vice, death, poverty, disease are weighty and grievous subjects. A soul should be schooled to bear up under evils and to argue with them, trained in the rules of living and believing well, and roused up often to exercise itself in this noble study. But for an ordinary soul this has to happen in intervals, and in moderation, or it will grow stupefied if always kept at it. When I was young I had to keep prodding myself, reminding myself, to hold to my duty: cheerfulness and good health, they say, do not go well with grave serious meditations. I am now in another state. The conditions of age keep reminding me, pressing me toward wisdom, preaching at me. I have fallen from an excess of liveliness into an excess of severity, which is much more troublesome — and for that reason I now and then deliberately let myself slip into a bit of disorder and occupy my mind with wanton and youthful thoughts to give it a holiday. Lately I have grown too reserved, too heavy, too ripe; the years read me daily lectures on coldness and temperance. This body of mine avoids disorder and dreads it: it is the body's turn now to lead the mind toward reformation; it governs in its turn, and more rudely and imperiously than the mind ever did; it lets me have no hour to myself, sleeping or waking, but is always preaching death, patience, repentance. I now defend myself against temperance as I used to defend myself against pleasure; it draws me too far back, even into a kind of stupidity. I will be master of myself in all things; wisdom too has its excesses, and stands as much in need of moderation as folly does. So, lest I wither, dry up, and overload myself with prudence, in the intervals and truces my infirmities allow me:
"Mens intenta suis ne seit usque malis."
["That my mind not be forever fixed on its ills." — Ovid, Trist., iv. 1, 4.]

I gently turn aside and avert my eyes from the stormy clouded sky in front of me — which, thank God, I look at without fear, but not without meditation and study — and amuse myself in the memory of my better years:
"Animus quo perdidit, optat, Atque in praeterita se totus imagine versat."
["The mind longs for what it has lost, and throws itself wholly into images of the past." — Petronius, c. 128.]

Let childhood look forward and age look back: was that not what Janus' double face meant? Let the years drag me along if they must, but let it be backward. As long as my eyes can still make out that pleasant season now expired, I will turn them that way from time to time; though it has fled from my blood and my veins, I will not let its image be uprooted from my memory:
"Hoc est Vivere bis, vita posse priore frui."
["It is to live twice, to be able to enjoy one's former life again." — Martial, x. 23, 7.]

Plato directs that old men should attend the exercises, dances, and sports of the young, that they may take joy in others for the bodily energy and beauty that is no longer in themselves, and recall the grace and comeliness of that blossoming age; and he wants the prize at these recreations to be awarded to whichever young man has most pleased the company. I used to mark the cloudy gloomy days as exceptional; now those are my ordinary days, and the extraordinary ones are the clear and bright. I am ready to leap for joy, as at some unusual favour, when nothing in particular goes wrong. Tickle me how you like, I cannot squeeze a smile out of this wretched body. I am cheerful only in fancy and dreaming, by some trick to divert the melancholy of age; but in truth that calls for another remedy than a dream. A feeble contest of art against nature. It is great folly to draw out and anticipate human troubles, as everyone does; I would rather be old for a shorter time than be old before I really am. I seize on even the smallest occasions of pleasure I can come across. I know, by hearsay, several sorts of prudent pleasures, genuinely such, and glorious too; but the reputation of them has no hold over me strong enough to give me an appetite for them. I do not so much want them magnanimous, magnificent, and pompous as I want them sweet, easy, and ready to hand:
"A natura discedimus; populo nos damus, nullius rei bono auctori."
["We depart from nature and give ourselves over to the crowd, who has nothing good to teach." — Seneca, Ep., 99.]
My philosophy is in action, in natural and immediate practice, very little in fancy: what if I should take pleasure in cracking nuts or whipping a top?
"Non ponebat enim rumores ante salutem."
["He did not put rumours ahead of his own health." — Ennius, in Cicero, De Offic., i. 24.]

Pleasure is a quality of very little ambition; it thinks itself rich enough by itself, without any boost in reputation, and is best pleased when retired from view. A young man ought to be whipped who sets himself up as a connoisseur of wines and sauces; at that age there was nothing I valued less or knew less. Now I am beginning to learn. I am very much ashamed of it — but what am I to do? I am more ashamed and vexed at the occasions that drive me to it. It is for us to dote and trifle the time away, and for young men to mind their reputation and stand on nice points; they are heading out into the world and the world's opinion, while we are retiring from it:
"Sibi arma, sibi equos, sibi hastas, sibi clavam, sibi pilam, sibi natationes, et cursus habeant: nobis senibus, ex lusionibus multis, talos relinquant et tesseras;"
["Let them keep for themselves the arms, horses, spears, clubs, ball games, swimming, and races; and out of all those sports leave to us old men cards and dice." — Cicero, De Senec., c. 16.]

the laws themselves send us home. I can do no less for this wretched state into which my age has thrown me than furnish it with toys to play with, as you do for a child; and in truth that is what we become. Wisdom and folly will both have plenty to do, taking turns to prop me up and ease me through this calamity of age:
"Misce stultitiam consiliis brevem."
["Mix a brief interval of folly with your counsels." — Horace, Od., iv. 12, 27.]
I accordingly avoid the lightest little pricks; the things that once would not have scratched the skin now go right through me. My body is so naturally inclining toward ill:
"In fragili corpore odiosa omnis offensio est;"
["In a fragile body every shock is hateful." — Cicero, De Senec., c. 18.]
"Mensque pati durum sustinet aegra nihil."
["And the sick mind can bear no hard exertion." — Ovid, De Ponto, i. 5, 18.]
I have always been very tender about offences; I am much more tender now, and exposed all over.
"Et minimae vires frangere quassa valent."
["Little force suffices to break what was already cracked." — Ovid, De Tris., iii. 11, 22.]

My judgment restrains me from kicking and grumbling at the inconveniences nature commands me to endure, but it does not take away my feeling them. I, whose only aim is to live and be merry, would run from one end of the world to the other to find one good year of pleasant cheerful tranquillity. A melancholy dull tranquillity may be enough for me, but it numbs me and stupefies me; I am not content with it. If there is any person, any little knot of good company, in country or city, in France or anywhere else, resident or on the move, who can take to my humour and whose humour I can take to, let them whistle and I will come running and furnish them with essays in flesh and bone:

Since it is the privilege of the mind to rescue itself from old age, I urge mine to do so with all the power I have. Let it stay green meanwhile and flourish if it can, like mistletoe on a dead tree. But I fear it is a traitor; it has contracted such a close brotherhood with the body that it leaves me at every turn to go follow the body in its need. I wheedle it apart in vain; I try in vain to wean it off this correspondence, to no effect; I quote Seneca and Catullus to it, and ladies and royal masques. If its companion has the stone, it seems to have it too; even those faculties most peculiarly its own cannot then perform their functions but appear stupefied and asleep. There is no liveliness in what it produces if the body is not in equal measure lively too.

Our schoolmasters are to blame, when they hunt for the causes of the soul's exceptional movements, that besides ascribing them to divine ecstasy, love, martial fury, poetry, or wine, they have not also assigned a share to health: a boiling, vigorous, full, easeful health, such as the greenness of youth and a sense of safety used to give me by fits. That fire of liveliness and gaiety throws into the mind flashes that are brighter and livelier than our natural light, and is, of all enthusiasms, the most jovial — if not the most extravagant.
So it is no wonder if the opposite state dulls and clogs my spirit, and produces the opposite effect:
"Ad nullum consurgit opus, cum corpore languet;"
["It rises to no effort; it languishes with the body." — Pseudo-Gallus, i. 125.]

and yet my mind expects me to be grateful for the fact that, as it would make out, it gives much less consent to this stupidity than is usual in men of my age. While we are in a truce, at least, let us drive incommodities and difficulties out of our exchanges:
"Dum licet, obducta solvatur fronte senectus:"
["While we can, let us banish old age from the brow." — Herodotus, Ep., xiii. 7.]
"Tetrica sunt amcenanda jocularibus."
["Sour things should be sweetened with pleasant ones." — Sidonius Apollinaris, Ep., i. 9.]
I love a gay civil wisdom and steer clear of all sourness and austerity of manner; any forbidding bearing is suspect to me:
"Tristemque vultus tetrici arrogantiam:"
["The gloomy arrogance of a crabbed face." — Anonymous.]
"Et habet tristis quoque turba cinaedos."
["An austere countenance sometimes covers a debauched mind." — Idem.]

I am very much of Plato's opinion, that easy or harsh humours are strong indications of the soul's good or ill disposition. Socrates had a steady countenance — but serene and smiling, not sourly austere like the elder Crassus, whom nobody ever saw laugh. Virtue is a pleasant and gay quality.

I know very well that few will quarrel with the licence of my writings who do not have more to quarrel with in the licence of their own thoughts. I conform myself well enough to their inclinations, but I offend their eyes. It is a fine humour they have, to strain Plato's writings and twist his supposed intimacies with Phaedo, Dion, Stella, and Archeanassa:
"Non pudeat dicere, quod non pudet sentire."
["Let us not be ashamed to say what we are not ashamed to think."]

I hate a sullen, peevish, dismal spirit that slides over all the pleasures of life and fastens itself only on misfortunes — like flies, which cannot stick to a smooth polished body but settle on craggy rough places, or like cupping-glasses that only suck up and attract bad blood.

As for the rest, I have set myself to dare to say everything I dare to do; even thoughts that should not be made public displease me. The worst of my actions and qualities do not look as evil to me as the evil and base business of not daring to own up to them. Everyone is wary and discreet in confession; men ought to be so in action. The boldness of doing ill is in some sort offset and held back by the boldness of confessing it. Whoever obliges himself to tell everything should oblige himself to do nothing he would be forced to conceal. I wish that this excess of licence in me would draw men toward freedom, above those timorous mincing virtues that grow out of our imperfections, and that at the expense of my immoderation I might bring them back to reason. A man must see and study his vice in order to correct it; those who hide it from others usually hide it from themselves, and don't think it well enough hidden if they themselves can see it: they pull back and disguise it from their own consciences:
"Quare vitia sua nemo confitetur? Quia etiam nunc in illia est; somnium narrare vigilantis est."
["Why does no one confess his vices? Because he is still in them; to tell a dream you have to be awake." — Seneca, Ep., 53.]

Diseases of the body declare themselves as they grow; we find that to be gout which we called a chill or a strain. Diseases of the soul, the worse they are, keep themselves the most hidden; the sickest are the least sensible of it. That is why they need to be taken to task with an unrelenting hand, opened up in broad daylight, and torn out of the hollow of the heart. As in doing well, so in doing ill, the mere confession is sometimes satisfaction in itself. Is there any deformity in doing wrong that can excuse us from confessing it? It is such a pain to me to dissemble that I avoid being trusted with other people's secrets, lacking the courage to disavow my knowledge of them. I can keep silent, but I cannot deny without the greatest possible difficulty and violence to myself. To be very secret a man must be so by nature, not by obligation. It is small worth, in serving a prince, to be secret if a man is not a liar to boot. If the man who asked Thales of Miletus whether he ought solemnly to deny that he had committed adultery had come to me, I would have told him he ought not to: I look on lying as a worse fault than the other. Thales gave the opposite advice, telling him to swear it, to shield the greater fault by the lesser;
[Montaigne's memory serves him ill here: when the question was put to Thales, his answer was, "But is perjury not worse than adultery?" — Diogenes Laertius, in Vita, i. 36.]

still, this counsel was not so much a choice as a multiplication of vice. Let us say in passing that we deal kindly with a man of conscience when we offer him some difficulty to weigh against a vice; but when we shut him in between two vices, he is put to a hard choice — as Origen was, either to commit idolatry or to let himself be carnally abused by a great Ethiopian slave they brought to him. He submitted to the first, and people say wrongly. Yet some women of our day are not so far off, in their own confusion, who declare they had rather burden their conscience with ten men than one mass.

If it is indiscreet to publish one's own errors like this, still there is no great danger that it will pass into example and custom — for Ariston said that the winds men most fear are those that lay them bare. We need to tuck up this ridiculous rag that hides our manners: they send their consciences to the brothel and keep a starched face; even traitors and assassins sign on to the laws of ceremony and locate their duty there. So that injustice cannot complain of being uncivil, nor malice of indiscretion. It is a pity but that a bad man should be a fool to boot, and that outward decency should paper over his vice: this rough-cast only belongs on a good sound wall, one that deserves to be preserved and whitewashed.

In favour of the Huguenots, who condemn our private auricular confession, I confess myself publicly, religiously and purely. St Augustine, Origen, and Hippocrates published the errors of their opinions; I, on top of that, of my conduct. I am greedy to make myself known, and I don't care to how many — provided it be truly. Or to put it better: I hunger for nothing; but I mortally hate to be mistaken by those who happen to learn my name. The man who does everything for honour and glory — what does he think he gains by showing himself to the world in a mask and concealing his real self from people? Praise a humpback for his stature: he has reason to take it as an insult. If you are a coward and people commend you for your valour, is it of you that they are speaking? They take you for somebody else. I would like as well the man who glorifies himself in the bows and salutations made to him as if he were master of the company, when he is one of the least of the retinue. Archelaus, king of Macedon, walking along the street, had water thrown on his head by someone, and his companions said he ought to punish them. "Well," he said, "whoever it was, he didn't throw water on me — but on the man he took me to be." Socrates, told that people spoke ill of him, said, "Not at all — there is nothing in me of what they say."

For my part, if anyone praised me as a good pilot, as a very modest man, or a very chaste one, I should owe him no thanks. And in the same way, whoever should call me traitor, robber, or drunkard, I should be as little troubled. They who do not really know themselves can feed on false approbations; not I, who see myself and examine myself even to my very bowels, and who know very well what I am owed. I am content to be less praised, provided I am better known. I may be reputed a wise man in the kind of wisdom I take to be folly. It vexes me that my Essays only serve the ladies as a common piece of furniture — a thing for the salon; this chapter will get me into the boudoir. I love to traffic with them a little in private; public conversation is without favour and without savour. At farewells we tend to warm our affections toward the things we are leaving; I take my last leave of the pleasures of this world: these are our last embraces.

But let us come to my subject. What has the act of generation, so natural, so necessary, so just, done to men, that we cannot speak of it without blushing, and that it is excluded from all serious and moderate discourse? We boldly say kill, rob, betray, and yet this one we dare only mention through our teeth. Is it because the less we spend in words, the more we can pay in thinking? For it is certain that the words least in use, least often written, and most carefully kept in are the best and most universally known; no age, no manners are ignorant of them, any more than they are of the word "bread"; they imprint themselves on everyone without being uttered, without sound, without picture; and the sex that practises this act most is bound to say least about it. It is an act we have placed in the franchise of silence, from which to remove it is a crime even to charge and judge it; nor do we dare correct it except by paraphrase and indirection. A great favour to a criminal, to be so execrable that justice thinks it unjust to touch him or look at him — free, and safe, by the severity of his condemnation. Is it not here as with books, which sell better and become more public for being suppressed? For my part, I will take Aristotle at his word, who says that "bashfulness is an ornament to youth, but a reproach to old age." These verses are preached in the old school, a school to which I adhere much more than to the modern: its virtues seem to me greater and its vices smaller:
"Ceux qui par trop fuyant Venus estrivent, Faillent autant que ceulx qui trop la suyvent."
["Those who flee Venus too strenuously err as much as those who too eagerly pursue her." — translation by Amyot from Plutarch, "A philosopher should converse with princes."]
"Tu, dea, rerum naturam sola gubernas, Nec sine to quicquam dias in luminis oras Exoritur, neque fit laetum, nec amabile quidquam."
["Goddess, you alone govern the nature of things; without you nothing comes into the shores of light, nothing pleasant, nothing lovely arises." — Lucretius, i. 22.]

I cannot imagine who could set Pallas and the Muses at variance with Venus and make them cold toward Love; I see no deities better met, or more indebted to each other. Whoever robs the Muses of amorous imaginings strips them of their best entertainment, and of the noblest matter of their work; whoever makes Love lose poetry's company and service disarms him of his best weapons. By doing so, they charge the god of intimacy and good will, and the protecting goddesses of humanity and justice, with the vice of ingratitude. I have not been so long cashiered from this god's army and service that my memory has lost its sharpness about his force and worth:
"Agnosco veteris vestigia flammae;"
["I recognise the traces of my old flame." — Aeneid, iv. 23.]
There are still some remnants of heat and emotion after the fever:
"Nec mihi deficiat calor hic, hiemantibus annis!"
["Nor may this heat of youth fail me in my winter years!"]
Withered and drooping as I am, I still feel some remains of that old ardour:
"Qual l'alto Egeo, per the Aquilone o Noto Cessi, the tutto prima il volse et scosse, Non 's accheta ei pero; ma'l suono e'l moto Ritien del l'onde anco agitate e grosse:"

["As the high Aegean, when the north or south wind has ceased after first stirring it through and through, does not settle yet; but holds the sound and motion of waves still agitated and swollen." — Tasso, in Fairfax's translation.]
but from what I know of it, the force and power of this god are more lively and animated in the picture poetry paints of him than in their own substance:
"Et versus digitos habet:"
["Verse has fingers." — adapted from Juvenal, iv. 196.]
It has some sort of air about it more amorous than love itself. Venus is not as beautiful, naked, alive, and panting as she is here in Virgil:

"Dixerat; et niveis hinc atque inde Diva lacertis Cunctantem amplexu molli fovet. Ille repente Accepit solitam flammam; notusque medullas Intravit calor, et labefacta per ossa cucurrit Non secus atque olim tonitru, cum rupta corusco Ignea rima micans percurrit lumine nimbos. . . . . . . Ea verba loquutus, Optatos dedit amplexus; placidumque petivit Conjugis infusus gremio per membra soporem."

["The goddess spoke, and throwing her snowy arms around him on both sides held him hesitating in a soft embrace. Suddenly he caught the accustomed flame; the familiar heat went through his marrow and ran thrilling through his shaken bones — just as when, with thunder, a stream of fire in lightning flashes shoots across the storm-clouds. Having said these words, he gave her the longed-for embrace, and sank into placid sleep on his wife's breast." — Aeneid, viii. 387 and 392.]

The only fault I find on considering it is that he has made her a little too passionate for a married Venus; in this discreet kind of coupling, the appetite is not usually so wanton, but graver and duller. Love hates that people should owe themselves to anything but itself, and goes only feebly to work in intimacies derived from any other title, like marriage, where alliance and dowry weigh as much as or more than grace and beauty. People do not marry for themselves, whatever they say; they marry just as much, or more, for their posterity and their family. The custom and interest of marriage concern our line much more than us, which is why I prefer a match arranged by a third hand rather than by the man himself, and to have another's liking rather than the party's own; and how opposed all that is to the conventions of love! It is also a kind of incest to bring into this venerable and sacred alliance the heat and extravagance of amorous licence, as I think I have said elsewhere. A man, Aristotle says, must approach his wife with prudence and temperance, lest in dealing too lasciviously with her, the extreme pleasure should make her step outside the bounds of reason. What he says on the score of conscience, the physicians say on the score of health: that a too lascivious, voluptuous, frequent pleasure makes the seed too hot and hinders conception. They say elsewhere that to give a languishing intercourse, such as this naturally is, the proper fertile heat, a man must do it but seldom and at appreciable intervals:
"Quo rapiat sitiens Venerem, interiusque recondat."
["That he may thirstily snatch the joys of love, and hold them more inwardly." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 137.]

I see no marriages where conjugal compatibility breaks down sooner than those we contract on the basis of beauty and amorous desire; there should be a more solid and constant foundation, and we should proceed with greater circumspection — this furious ardour is worth nothing.

Those who think they honour marriage by joining love to it, do, it seems to me, just like those who, to honour virtue, hold that nobility is nothing else but virtue. They are indeed things with some relation to one another, but there is a great deal of difference; we should not so mix their names and titles; it does a wrong to both to confound them. Nobility is a fine quality, and rightly introduced; but since it is a quality depending on others, and may turn up in a vicious person, in himself nothing, it stands infinitely below virtue in real value;
["If nobility be virtue, it loses its quality in everything in which it is not virtuous: and if it is not virtue, it is a small matter." — La Bruyère.]

it is a virtue, if it is one at all, that is artificial and apparent, depending on time and luck; various in form according to the country; living and mortal; without birth, like the river Nile; genealogical and common; got by succession and similitude; drawn by consequence, and a weak one. Knowledge, strength, goodness, beauty, riches, and all other qualities enter into trade and exchange; this one is consummated in itself and is of no use to others. There was offered to one of our kings the choice of two candidates for the same command, one a gentleman, the other not; he ordered that without respect to quality they should choose the one with the most merit, but where the worth of the candidates was equal, they should have regard to birth. That was rightly to give it its rank. A young man unknown came to Antigonus to apply for his father's command — his father a brave man lately dead. "Friend," he said, "in such promotions I have not so much regard to the nobility of my soldiers as to their prowess." And indeed, it should not go as it did with the officers of the kings of Sparta — trumpeters, fiddlers, cooks, whose children always succeeded to their places, however ignorant, and were preferred over the most experienced in the trade. The people of Calicut treat their nobles as a sort of superhuman beings: they are forbidden marriage and any but warlike employment; they may have all the concubines they want, and the women as many lovers, without anyone being jealous; but it is a capital, unforgivable crime to couple with anyone of lower condition than themselves. They count themselves polluted if they have so much as touched one in walking past; and reckoning their nobility prodigiously interested and injured in it, they kill anyone who comes too close. So the lowborn have to call out as they go, like the gondoliers of Venice at the turns of streets, for fear of jostling, and the nobles command them to step aside whenever they please. By this means the nobles avoid what they consider perpetual disgrace, and the others avoid certain death. No time, no favour of the prince, no office, virtue, or riches can ever make a commoner become a noble; and to this another custom contributes — that marriages between different trades are forbidden: the daughter of a cordwainer's guild is not allowed to marry a carpenter, and parents are obliged to train their children strictly in their own callings and not put them to any other trade; this is how the distinction and continuance of their stations are maintained.

A good marriage, if there is any such thing, rejects the company and conditions of love, and tries to represent those of friendship. It is a sweet society of life, full of constancy, trust, and an infinite number of useful and solid services and mutual obligations; which any woman of right taste:
"Optato quam junxit lumine taeda" —
["Whom the marriage torch has joined with the longed-for light." — Catullus, lxiv. 79.]

would be loth to serve her husband in the role of a mistress. If she is lodged in his affection as a wife, she is more honourably and securely placed. When he sets out to be in love with another, and does all he can to obtain his desire, just ask him on which of them he had rather a disgrace should fall, his wife or his mistress; which of their misfortunes would most afflict him, and to which of them he wishes most distinction; the answer is not in doubt in a sound marriage.

And the fact that so few are seen to be happy is a sign of its preciousness and value. If well formed and rightly taken, it is the best of all human societies; we cannot live without it, and yet we do nothing but slander it. As with cages, the birds outside despair of getting in, and those within despair of getting out. Socrates, asked whether it was more advisable to take a wife or not, said, "Let a man take whichever course he will; he will repent." It is a contract to which the common saying:
"Homo homini aut deus aut lupus,"
["Man to man is either a god or a wolf." — Erasmus, Adag.]

may very fitly be applied; there has to be a concurrence of many qualities in the construction. It is found these days more convenient for simple plebeian souls, where delights, curiosity, and idleness do not disturb it so much; but extravagant humours such as mine, that hate all sorts of obligation and restraint, are not so suited to it:
"Et mihi dulce magis resoluto vivere collo."
["It is sweeter for me to live with a loosened neck." — Pseudo-Gallus, i. 61.]

If I had my own way, I would not have married Wisdom herself, if she would have had me. But there is no use evading it; the common custom and use of life will have it so. Most of my actions are guided by example, not choice, and yet I did not enter into it by my own voluntary motion; I was led and drawn into it by extrinsic occasions. For not only things that are inconvenient in themselves, but also things ugly, vicious, and to be avoided, can be made acceptable by some condition or accident — so unsteady and vain is all human resolution. And I was persuaded to it when I was less ready and less tractable than I am now that I have tried what it is; and as great a libertine as I am taken to be, I have in truth more strictly observed the laws of marriage than I either promised or expected. It is no use kicking once a man has put on his fetters: a man must prudently manage his liberty, but having once submitted to obligation, he must hold himself within the laws of common duty, or at least do what he can toward it. Those who enter into this contract intending to behave in it with hatred and contempt do an unjust and uncomfortable thing; and the fine rule I hear passed from hand to hand among the women, as a sacred oracle:
["Serve thy husband as thy master, but guard thyself against him as from a traitor."]

— which is to say, conduct yourself toward him with a dissembled, hostile, distrustful reverence (a war-cry and a defiance) — is equally injurious and harsh. I am too mild for such rough designs; to tell the truth, I have not arrived at that perfection of cleverness and refinement which lets one confound reason with injustice, and laugh at any rule or order that does not please my palate; because I hate superstition, I do not at once fall into the opposite extreme of irreligion.
(If a man hates superstition, he cannot love religion.)
If a man does not always perform his duty, he ought at least to love and acknowledge it; it is treachery to marry without marrying in spirit.
Let us proceed.

Our poet represents a marriage happy in a good accord wherein nevertheless there is not much loyalty. Does he mean that it is not impossible for a woman to give the reins to her own passion, yield to the importunities of love, and yet keep some duty toward marriage — and that it may be hurt without being totally broken? A servant can cheat his master without hating him. Beauty, opportunity, and destiny (for destiny too has a hand in it),
"Fatum est in partibus illis Quas sinus abscondit; nam, si tibi sidera cessent, Nil faciet longi mensura incognita nervi;"
["There is a fatality about the hidden parts: let nature have endowed you ever so liberally, it does no good if your good star fails you in the moment." — Juvenal, ix. 32.]

may have attached her to a stranger — though not so wholly, perhaps, but that she may still have some remains of kindness for her husband. They are two designs, with several paths leading to them, that need not be confused with each other; a woman can yield to a man she would by no means have married, not only for the condition of his fortune but for those of his person too. Few men have made a wife of a mistress without repenting it. And even in the other world, what an unhappy life Jupiter has with his, whom he had first enjoyed as a mistress! It is, as the proverb says, to dirty a basket and then put it on one's head. I have in my time, in a good family, seen a love shamefully and dishonestly cured by marriage: the considerations involved are altogether different. We love at once, without any tie, two things that are contraries.

Socrates used to say that the city of Athens pleased people the way ladies do whom men court for love: everyone loved to come there to take a turn and pass the time, but no one liked it well enough to marry it — that is, to live there and make it his constant residence. I have been vexed to see husbands hate their wives merely because they themselves wrong them. We should not, at all events, love them less for our own faults; if anything, on account of repentance and pity, they should be dearer to us.

They are different ends, he says, and yet in some sort compatible; marriage has utility, justice, honour, and constancy for its share — a flat but more universal pleasure. Love founds itself wholly on pleasure, and indeed has it more full, lively, and sharp — a pleasure inflamed by difficulty; there must be in it sting and smart; it is no longer love if without darts and fire. The bounty of ladies is too profuse in marriage and dulls the point of affection and desire; to get round this inconvenience, just look at the pains Lycurgus and Plato take in their laws.

Women are not at all to blame when they refuse the rules of life that are brought into the world, since men make these rules without their help. There is naturally contention and squabbling between them and us; even the closest friendship we have with them is mixed with tumult and tempest. In our author's opinion, we deal carelessly with them in this regard: after we have discovered that they are, beyond comparison, more capable and more ardent in the practice of love than we are, and that the old priest testified as much, who had once been a man and then a woman:
"Venus huic erat utraque nota:"
["Both aspects of love were known to him." — Tiresias, Ovid, Metam., iii. 323.]

and that, moreover, we have learned from their own mouths the proof made in various ages by an emperor and an empress of Rome, both famous for ability in that affair: for he in one night deflowered ten Sarmatian virgins among his captives; but she had twenty-five bouts in one night, changing partners as her need and liking required;
"Adhuc ardens rigidae tentigine vulvae Et lassata viris, nondum satiata, recessit:"
["Still burning, she withdrew, tired but not satisfied." — Juvenal, vi. 128.]

and given the case that arose in Catalonia, where a wife complained of her husband's too frequent attentions — not so much, I should think, because she was put out by it (I don't believe in miracles outside religion) as under that pretext, to curtail and curb the husband's authority over his wife in this fundamental act of marriage, and to show that their hostility and malice go beyond the nuptial bed and trample even on the graces and sweets of Venus; the husband, a truly brutish and unnatural man, answered that even on fasting days he could not subsist with less than ten goes — out of which came the famous judgment of the Queen of Aragon, by which, after mature deliberation by her council, this good queen, to give a rule and example to all succeeding ages of the moderation required in a just marriage, set down six times a day as a legitimate and necessary stint; surrendering and giving up a great deal of the needs and desires of her sex, that she might, she said, establish an easy, and therefore a permanent and immutable, rule. To which the doctors exclaim: what must the female appetite and concupiscence be, when their reason, their reformation, their virtue, are taxed at such a rate? Considering the various judgments of our appetites — for Solon, master of the law school, taxes us at only three a month, lest men fail in point of conjugal frequency — after having, I say, believed and preached all this, we go and enjoin them to continency, on the harshest and most extreme penalties.

There is no passion so hard to contend with as this, which we would have them alone resist, and not as an ordinary vice but as an execrable abomination, worse than irreligion or parricide; while we, at the same time, go at it without reproach or offence. Even those among us who have tried the experiment have confessed sufficiently what difficulty, or rather impossibility, they have found in subduing, weakening, and cooling the body by material remedies. We, on the contrary, would have them sound, vigorous, plump, well-fed, and chaste; that is to say, both hot and cold. For the marriage we tell them is to keep them from burning is only a small refreshment to them, given how we run the business. If they take a husband whose vigorous age is still on the boil, he will be proud to make it known elsewhere;
"Sit tandem pudor; aut eamus in jus; Multis mentula millibus redempta, Non est haec tua, Basse; vendidisti;"
["Have some shame at last, or we shall go to law: your vigour, bought by your wife with many thousands, is no longer yours, Bassus; you have sold it." — Martial, xii. 90.]

Polemon the philosopher was rightly brought before the judge by his wife for sowing in a barren field the seed that was due to a fruitful one. If, on the other hand, they take a husband whose strength is gone, they are in a worse condition in marriage than maids or widows. We think them well provided for because they have a man to sleep with — as the Romans concluded that Clodia Laeta, a vestal nun, had been violated because Caligula had approached her, although it was declared he did no more than approach. But on the contrary, in this way we increase their need, since the touch and company of any man whatever rouses their desires, which in solitude would be quieter. And, it would seem, to render their chastity more meritorious by such a circumstance, Boleslas and his wife Kinge, kings of Poland, vowed it by mutual consent in bed together on their very wedding day, and kept the vow in spite of every matrimonial convenience.

We train them up from infancy in the traffic of love; their grace, dress, knowledge, language, and entire instruction is bent that way. Their governesses imprint nothing on them but the idea of love, if only by continually representing it to them, even pretending to give them a distaste for it. My daughter, my only child, is now of an age that forward young women are allowed to be married at. She is of a slow, thin, tender constitution, and has been brought up by her mother accordingly, in a secluded private way, so that she is only now beginning to be weaned from her childish simplicity. She was reading before me in a French book where the word "fouteau" — the name of a tree, as it happens — occurred; the woman in charge of her stopped her short rather sharply and made her skip the dangerous syllables. I let her alone, not to disturb their rules, for I never meddle in that sort of management; feminine politics has a mysterious procedure; we must leave it to them. But unless I am mistaken, the company of twenty footmen could not, in six months, have so imprinted in her memory the meaning, usage, and all the consequences of those naughty syllables, as that good old woman did by her reprimand and ban.
"Motus doceri gaudet Ionicos Matura virgo, et frangitur artibus; Jam nunc et incestos amores De tenero, meditatur ungui."

["The maid ripe for marriage takes pleasure in being taught Ionic dances and is bent in lascivious motions. Why, already from her tender years she meditates on criminal loves." — Horace, Od., iii. 6, 21; the text has "fingitur."]

Let them just give themselves a little rein, let them just enter into liberty of conversation, and we are children compared to them in this science. Listen to them describe our pursuits and our talk, and they will make you understand very well that we bring them nothing they have not already known and digested without our help.

[This sentence refers to a conversation between some young women in his immediate neighbourhood, which Montaigne tells us just below he overheard, and which he found too shocking to repeat. It must have been fairly bad.]

Is it perhaps, as Plato says, that they were formerly debauched young men? I happened one day to be somewhere I could hear some of their talk without their suspecting it; I am sorry I cannot repeat it. By my faith, I said, we had better go and study the phrases of Amadis and the tales of Boccaccio and Aretino, to be able to keep up with them; we are putting our time to good use indeed. There is no word, no example, no step, that they are not more practised in than our books are; it is a discipline that springs from their blood:
"Et mentem ipsa Venus dedit,"
["Venus herself made them what they are." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 267.]
which those good instructors, nature, youth, and health, are continually inspiring them with. They have no need to learn it; they breed it:
"Nec tantum niveo gavisa est ulla columbo, Compar, vel si quid dicitur improbius, Oscula mordenti semper decerpere rostro, Quantum praecipue multivola est mulier."
["No milk-white dove, or if there is anything more lascivious, takes such delight in kissing as woman, eager for every man she sees." — Catullus, lxvi. 125.]

So that if the natural violence of their desire were not somewhat restrained by fear and honour, which were wisely contrived for them, we would all be shamed. All the motions in the world resolve into this conjunction and tend toward it; it is a matter that runs through everything; it is a centre toward which all things are pulled. We still see the edicts of old wise Rome made in the service of love, and Socrates' precepts for the instruction of courtesans:
"Noncon libelli Stoici inter sericos Jacere pulvillos amant:"
["There are writings of the Stoics which we find lying upon silken cushions." — Horace, Epod., viii. 15.]

Zeno also, among his laws, regulated the motions to be used in deflowering a maiden. What was the philosopher Strato's book "Of Carnal Conjunction"? What did Theophrastus treat of in the books he entitled "The Lover" and "Of Love"? Or Aristippus in his "Of Former Delights"? What do those long lively descriptions in Plato of the loves of his time aim at? Or the book called "The Lover" by Demetrius of Phalerum? Or "Clinias," or "The Ravished Lover," by Heraclides? Or Antisthenes's "Of Getting Children," or "Of Weddings," and the other, "Of the Master or the Lover"? Or Aristo's "Of Amorous Exercises"? Or those of Cleanthes, one "Of Love," the other "Of the Art of Loving"? The amorous dialogues of Sphaerus? And Chrysippus' fable of Jupiter and Juno, impudent beyond tolerance? And his fifty so-lascivious epistles? I will leave aside the writings of the philosophers of the Epicurean sect, protectress of voluptuousness. In time past, fifty deities were assigned to this office; and there have been nations where, to assuage the lust of those who came to their devotions, they kept men and women in their temples for the worshippers to lie with, and it was an act of ceremony to do this before going to prayer:
"Nimirum propter continentiam incontinentia necessaria est; incendium ignibus extinguitur."
["Of course, for continence's sake incontinence is necessary; a fire is put out by fires."]

In most of the world, that member of our body was deified; in the same province, some flayed the skin off it to offer and consecrate a piece; others offered and consecrated their seed. In another place, the young men publicly cut through, between the skin and the flesh of that part, in several places, and pushed pieces of wood into the openings as long and thick as they would receive, and afterwards made a fire of those pieces of wood as an offering to their gods; they were reckoned neither vigorous nor chaste if by the force of that cruel pain they showed any dismay. Elsewhere the most sacred magistrate was reverenced and acknowledged by that member, and in various ceremonies an effigy of it was carried in procession in honour of various deities. The Egyptian ladies, in their Bacchanalia, each carried one finely carved of wood about their necks, as large and heavy as she could so carry; besides which, the statue of their god presented one which surpassed all the rest of his body in size. The married women in the region where I live make of their kerchiefs the figure of one upon their foreheads, to glorify themselves in their enjoyment of it, and on becoming widows they throw it behind and cover it with their head-cloths. The most modest matrons of Rome thought it an honour to offer flowers and garlands to the god Priapus, and they made the virgins, at the time of their espousals, sit upon his shameful parts. And I am not sure I have not in my own time seen some air of similar devotion. What was the meaning of that ridiculous bit of our forefathers' clothing — and still worn by our Swiss? Why do we make a show of our equipment in figure under our breeches, and often, even worse, above its natural size, by falsehood and imposture? I have half a mind to believe that this sort of garment was invented in those better, more conscientious ages, that the world might not be deceived, and that every man should give a public account of his proportions. The simple peoples wear them still, and around their real size. Back then, the tailor took measure of it as the shoemaker now does of a man's foot. That worthy man who, when I was young, gelded so many noble and ancient statues in his great city, so they should not corrupt the eyesight of the ladies — following the advice of this other ancient worthy:
"Flagitii principium est, nudare inter gives corpora,"
["To strip the body before others is the beginning of wickedness." — Ennius, in Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 33.]
should have remembered that, as in the mysteries of the Bona Dea every masculine appearance was excluded, he did nothing if he did not also geld horses and donkeys — in short, all of nature:
"Omne adeo genus in terris, hominumque, ferarumque, Et genus aequoreum, pecudes, pictaeque volucres, In furias ignemque ruunt."
["So every kind of living thing on earth — men, beasts, wild or tame, fish, and gaudy fowl — rush to this flame of love." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 244.]

The gods, Plato says, have given us one disobedient and unruly member that, like a furious animal, attempts by the violence of its appetite to subject everything to it; and they have given to women one like a greedy and ravenous animal, which, if refused food in season, grows wild, impatient of delay, and infusing its rage into their bodies, blocks the passages, hinders breathing, and causes a thousand ills, until, having drunk in the fruit of the common thirst, it has plentifully bedewed the bottom of their matrix. Now my legislator might have considered that perhaps it would be a chaster and more fruitful course to let them know the fact as it is, in good time, rather than allow them to guess according to the liberty and heat of their own fancy. In place of the real parts, they substitute, through hope and desire, others that are three times more outsized; and a certain friend of mine ruined himself by producing his in the wrong place and at the wrong time. What harm those pictures of prodigious proportions do that the boys make on the stairs and galleries of the royal houses — they give the ladies a cruel contempt for our natural furniture. And how do we know but that Plato, after other well-ordered republics, decreed that men and women, old and young, should expose themselves naked to each other's view in his gymnastic exercises, on that very account? The Indian women who see the men in their natural state have at least cooled the sense of sight. And let the women of the kingdom of Pegu say what they will — they who below the waist have nothing to cover them but a cloth slit at the front, and so narrow that whatever decency and modesty they pretend by it, at every step everything is to be seen — it is an invention to draw the men to them and divert them from boys, to whom that nation is generally inclined. Yet perhaps they lose more by it than they gain, and one may venture to say that a whole appetite is sharper than one already half-glutted by the eyes. Livia used to say that to a virtuous woman, a naked man was only a statue. The Spartan women, more virgins as wives than our daughters are, saw every day the young men of their city stripped naked in their exercises, and themselves bothered little to cover their thighs in walking, believing themselves, as Plato says, sufficiently covered by their virtue, without any other robe. But those of whom St Augustine speaks have given nudity a wonderful power of temptation, who have made it a question whether women at the day of judgment will rise again in their own sex and not rather in ours, for fear of tempting us again even in that holy state. In short, we lure them and stir them up by every kind of means; we ceaselessly heat and stir up their imagination, and then we find fault. Let us confess the truth: there is scarcely one of us who does not more fear the shame that comes to him from his wife's vices than from his own, and is not more solicitous — wonderful charity! — about the conscience of his virtuous wife than about his own; who would not rather commit theft and sacrilege, and that his wife was a murderess and a heretic, than that she should not be more chaste than her husband. An unjust assessment of vices. Both we and they are capable of a thousand corruptions more harmful and unnatural than lust; but we weigh vices not according to nature, but according to our interest, by which they take so many unequal shapes.

The austerity of our decrees makes women's application to this vice more violent and vicious than its own nature requires, and entangles it in worse consequences than its causes warranted. They will readily go off to the courts to seek gain, or to the wars to win reputation, rather than, in the midst of ease and pleasures, have to mount such a difficult guard. Do they not see well enough that there is neither merchant nor soldier who will not leave his business to run after this sport — nor any porter or cobbler, however tired and worn down by labour and hunger?

"Num tu, qux tenuit dives Achaemenes, Aut pinguis Phrygiae Mygdonias opes, Permutare velis crine Licymnim? Plenas aut Arabum domos, Dum fragrantia detorquet ad oscula Cervicem, aut facili sxvitia negat, Quae poscente magis gaudeat eripi, Interdum rapere occupet?"

["Would you not exchange all that wealthy Achaemenes had, or the Mygdonian riches of fertile Phrygia, for one ringlet of Licymnia's hair? Or the treasures of the Arabians, when she turns her head to you for fragrant kisses, or with easily appeased anger denies them — which she would rather you took by force, and sometimes herself snatches first?" — Horace, Od., ii. 12, 21.]

I do not know whether the exploits of Alexander and Caesar really surpass the resolution of a beautiful young woman, brought up after our fashion in the daylight and traffic of the world, assailed by so many contrary examples, and still keeping herself entire in the midst of a thousand continual and powerful solicitations. There is no doing more difficult than that not-doing, nor more active.
I hold it easier to carry a suit of armour all the days of one's life than a maidenhead; and the vow of virginity is the noblest of all, as being the hardest to keep:
"Diaboli virtus in lumbis est,"

St Jerome says. We have, without doubt, given over to the ladies the most difficult and most strenuous of all human endeavours; let us give them the glory of it too. This ought to encourage them to be obstinate in it; it is a brave thing for them to defy us, and to spurn underfoot that vain pre-eminence of valour and virtue that we claim over them. They will find, if they notice it, that they will not only be much more esteemed for it but also much more loved. A gallant man does not give up his pursuit because he has been refused, provided it is a refusal of chastity and not of personal choice. We may swear, threaten, and complain all we like — we are only lying; we love them all the better for it. There is no allurement like modesty, if it is not rude and sour. It is stupidity and meanness to be stubborn in the face of hatred and disdain; but against a virtuous and constant resolution mixed with goodwill, that is the exercise of a noble and generous soul. They may acknowledge our service to a certain degree and give us civilly to understand that they do not disdain us; for the law that commands them to abhor us because we adore them, and to hate us because we love them, is certainly very cruel — if only for the difficulty of it. Why should they not lend an ear to our offers and requests, so long as they are kept within the bounds of modesty? Why should we imagine them to have other thoughts within, and to be worse than they seem? A queen of our time said wittily that to refuse these courtesies is a sign of weakness in women, and a self-accusation of being easy; and that a lady could not boast of her chastity who had never been tempted.

The limits of honour are not cut so short; they may give themselves a little rein and relax a little without being at fault: there lies on the frontier some space free, indifferent, and neutral. Whoever has beaten and pursued her into her fort is a strange fellow if he is not satisfied with his luck; the price of the conquest is reckoned by the difficulty. Would you know what impression your service and merit have made on her heart? Judge by her behaviour. Such a woman may grant more, who does not grant as much. The obligation of a favour relates wholly to the goodwill of those who confer it; the other circumstances that go with it are mute, dead, and accidental; it costs her dearer to grant you that little than it would cost her companion to grant everything. If rarity gives value to anything, it ought especially to in this; do not consider how little is given, but how few have it to give. The value of money changes according to the coinage and stamp of the place. Whatever the spite and indiscretion of some may make them say in the excess of their discontent, virtue and truth will in time recover all the advantage. I have known some whose reputation has long suffered under slander, who have afterwards been restored to universal approval by their mere constancy, without care or artifice; everyone repents and contradicts what he had believed and said, and women a little suspected as girls have afterward been advanced to the first rank among ladies of honour. Somebody told Plato that all the world spoke ill of him. "Let them talk," he said. "I will live in such a way as to make them change their tune." Besides the fear of God and the value of so rare a glory, which ought to make them look to themselves, the corruption of the age we live in compels them to it; if I were they, there is nothing I would not sooner do than entrust my reputation to such dangerous hands. In my time, the pleasure of telling — a pleasure little inferior to that of doing — was permitted only to those who had some faithful, single friend; but now ordinary conversation and common table-talk is nothing but boasts of favours received and of the secret generosity of ladies. In earnest, it is too abject, too mean-spirited, in men to allow such ungrateful, indiscreet, and giddy people so to persecute, forage, and pillage those tender and charming favours.
This our immoderate and illegitimate exasperation against this vice springs from the most vain and tumultuous disease that afflicts human minds, which is jealousy:
"Quis vetat apposito lumen de lumine sumi? Dent licet assidue, nil tamen inde perit;"
["Who says that one light should not be lighted from another light? Let them give ever so much; as much always remains to lose." — Ovid, De Arte Amandi, iii. 93.]

she and envy, her sister, seem to me the most foolish of the whole troop. Of envy I can say little; it is a passion that, though said to be so mighty and powerful, has never had anything to do with me. As for the other, I know it by sight, and that is all. Beasts feel it. The shepherd Cratis, having fallen in love with a she-goat, was found one day by the he-goat — out of jealousy — and the he-goat butted his head as he lay asleep, and crushed it. We have raised this fever to a greater extreme by the examples of some barbarous nations; the best-disciplined have felt it too, and rightly, but not been carried away by it:
"Ense maritali nemo confossus adulter Purpureo Stygias sanguine tinxit aquas."
["Never did an adulterer slain by a husband stain the Stygian waters with purple blood."]

Lucullus, Caesar, Pompey, Antony, Cato, and other brave men were cuckolds, and knew it without making any fuss about it. In those days there was only one fool, Lepidus, who died of grief because his wife had treated him so.
"Ah! tum te miserum malique fati, Quem attractis pedibus, patente porta, Percurrent raphanique mugilesque:"
["Ah, wretched man of evil fate! when, taken in the act, you will be dragged out by the heels, and suffer the adulterer's punishment." — Catullus, xv. 17.]
And the god in our poet, when he caught one of his companions with his wife, contented himself with putting them to shame,
"Atque aliquis de dis non tristibus optat Sic fieri turpis:"
["And one of the more cheerful gods wishes he himself might be so disgraced." — Ovid, Metam., iv. 187.]
and nonetheless took offence at the lukewarm embraces she gave him, complaining that on that account she had grown jealous of his affection:
"Quid causas petis ex alto? fiducia cessit Quo tibi, diva, mei?"
["Why do you seek causes from on high? Goddess, where has your confidence in me gone?" — Virgil, Aeneid, viii. 395.]
Indeed she begs arms for a bastard of hers,
"Arena rogo genitrix nato."
["I, a mother, ask armour for a son." — Idem, ibid., 383.]
which are freely granted; and Vulcan speaks honourably of Aeneas:
"Arma acri facienda viro,"
["Arms must be made for a brave hero." — Aeneid, viii. 441.]
with, in truth, a more than human humanity. And I am content to leave this excess of kindness to the gods:
"Nec divis homines componier aequum est."
["Nor is it right to compare men with gods." — Catullus, lxviii. 141.]
As for the confusion of children, besides that the gravest legislators decree and approve it in their republics, it does not trouble the women, in whom this passion is, somehow, much better seated:
"Saepe etiam Juno, maxima coelicolam, Conjugis in culpa flagravit quotidiana."
["Often even Juno, greatest of the dwellers in heaven, was enraged by her husband's daily infidelities." — Idem, ibid.]

When jealousy seizes these poor souls, weak and incapable of resistance, it is a pity to see how miserably it torments and tyrannises over them; it slips in under the title of friendship, but once it has possessed them, the same causes that served as the foundation of goodwill now serve as the foundation of mortal hatred. Of all the diseases of the mind, it is the one that the most things serve to feed and the fewest to relieve. The virtue, health, merit, and reputation of the husband are kindling for her fury and ill-will:
"Nullae sunt inimicitiae, nisi amoris, acerbae."
["No hatreds are bitter except those of love." — Propertius, ii. 8, 3.]

This fever defaces and corrupts everything beautiful and good in her besides; and there is no action of a jealous woman, however chaste and however good a housewife she may be, that does not taste of anger and wrangling. It is a furious agitation, which throws her into an extremity quite opposite to its cause. This held good with one Octavius at Rome. After lying with Pontia Posthumia, he found his love grew by the enjoyment, and importuned her with every plea to marry him; unable to persuade her, this excessive affection threw him headlong into the effects of the most cruel and mortal hatred: he killed her. In the same way, the ordinary symptoms of this other amorous disease are internal hatreds, private conspiracies, and intrigues:
"Notumque furens quid faemina possit,"
["And it is known what a furious woman can do." — Aeneid, v. 21.]
and a rage which frets itself the more, as it is forced to excuse itself under the pretence of goodwill.

Now, the duty of chastity is of vast extent. Is it the will we want them to restrain? That is a very supple and active thing, very nimble and hard to bring to a stop. What if dreams sometimes carry them off so far they cannot refuse? It is not in them, nor perhaps in chastity itself, since chastity is feminine, to defend itself from lust and desire. If we are only to trust to their will, what a case are we in then? Just imagine what a crowd of men would be in pursuit of the privilege to run full speed, without tongue or eyes, into the arms of any woman who would have them. The Scythian women put out the eyes of all their slaves and prisoners of war, so they might have their pleasure of them without their being any the wiser. Oh, the furious advantage of opportunity! If anyone should ask me what is the first thing to be considered in matters of love, I would say it is how to take a fitting time; and the second; and the third — it is a point that does everything. I have sometimes lacked fortune, but sometimes I have been lacking to myself in matters of attempt. God help the man who still makes light of this. There is greater rashness required in our age — something our young men excuse under the name of heat; but should women examine it more strictly, they would find it springs from contempt rather. I was always superstitiously afraid of giving offence, and have always had great respect for the one I loved; besides, whoever takes away the reverence in this traffic also defaces the lustre. I would have a man, in this affair, be a little childish, a little timorous, a little servile. If not in this, I have in other matters something of that bashfulness Plutarch speaks of, and the course of my life has been damaged and blemished by it in various ways — a quality very ill-suited to my general make-up; and what are we, indeed, but contradiction and inconsistency? I am as much out of countenance to be denied as I am to deny; and it troubles me so much to put others to trouble that, on occasions when duty obliges me to test the goodwill of any one of them in a doubtful matter that will be a burden to him, I do it very faintly and very much against the grain. But if it is for my own particular interest (whatever Homer truly says, that modesty is a foolish virtue in a needy person), I commonly commit it to a third person to blush for me, and to refuse those who employ me with the same reluctance. So that it has sometimes happened that I had a mind to refuse but lacked the power to do it.

It is folly, then, to try to bridle in women a desire so powerful in them and so natural to them. And when I hear them boast of having such a maidenly and temperate will, I laugh at them. They retire too far back. If it is an old toothless hag, or a young dried-up consumptive thing, though it may not be wholly believable, at least they say it with some plausibility. But those who still move and breathe, talking at that ridiculous rate, do so to their own prejudice — because inconsiderate excuses are a kind of self-accusation. Like a gentleman, a neighbour of mine, suspected of impotence:
"Languidior tenera cui pendens sicula beta, Numquam se mediam sustulit ad tunicam,"
[Catullus, lxvii. 2, i. — The sense is given by the context.]

who, three or four days after he was married, went around boldly swearing, to clear himself, that he had ridden twenty stages the previous night — an oath that was afterwards used to convict him of his unfitness in that affair, and to divorce him from his wife. Besides, it means nothing, for there is neither continence nor virtue where there are no opposing desires. It is true, they may say, but we will not yield. Saints themselves speak in that manner — I mean those who boast in good gravity of their coldness and insensibility, and expect to be believed with a serious face. For when it is spoken with an affected look, when their eyes give the lie to their tongue, and when they talk in the cant of their profession, which always goes against the grain, it is rare sport. I am a great servant of liberty and plainness, but there is no remedy: if it is not wholly simple or childish, it is silly and unbecoming to ladies in this commerce, and runs straightaway into impudence. Their disguises and figures only serve to fool fools; lying is there in its seat of honour. It is a back-way that, by a side-door, leads us to truth. If we cannot curb their imagination, what do we want from them? Their actions? There are plenty of those that evade all outside communication, by which chastity may be corrupted:
"Illud saepe facit, quod sine teste facit;"
["He often does that which he does without a witness." — Martial, vii. 62, 6.]
and those we fear least are perhaps most to be feared; the sins that make the least noise are the worst:
"Offendor maecha simpliciore minus."
["I am less offended by an open-living strumpet." — Idem, vi. 7, 6.]
There are ways by which they may lose their virginity without prostitution, and, what is more, without their own knowledge:
"Obsterix, virginis cujusdam integritatem manu velut explorans, sive malevolentia, sive inscitia, sive casu, dum inspicit, perdidit."
["By malevolence, or unskilfulness, or accident, the midwife, while testing some maiden's virginity with her hand, has sometimes destroyed it." — St Augustine, De Civit. Dei, i. 18.]

Such a one, looking for her maidenhead, has lost it; another, playing with it, has destroyed it. We cannot precisely circumscribe the actions we forbid; they must guess at our meaning under general and doubtful terms. The very idea we invent of their chastity is ridiculous: among the highest patterns I have is Fatua, the wife of Faunus, who, after her marriage, never again let herself be seen by any man whatever; and the wife of Hiero, who never noticed her husband's stinking breath, imagining it common to all men. They have to become insensible and invisible to satisfy us.

Now, let us confess that the knot of this judgment of duty principally lies in the will. There have been husbands who suffered cuckoldom not only without reproach or taking offence at their wives, but with a sense of being singularly obliged to them, and great praise of their virtue. There has been such a woman, who valued her honour above her life, and yet has prostituted it to the raging lust of a mortal enemy to save her husband's life, and who, in so doing, did that for him she would not have done for herself. This is not the place to multiply such examples; they are too high and rich to be set off with so poor a foil as I can give them here; let us save them for a nobler place. But for examples of ordinary lustre, do we not see every day women among us who surrender themselves for their husbands' sole benefit, by their husbands' express order and mediation? And of old, Phaulius the Argive, who offered his wife to King Philip out of ambition; or Galba, who did it out of courtesy: having entertained Maecenas at supper, and noticing that his wife and Maecenas began to cast glances at each other and to exchange signs, Galba let himself sink down on his cushion like a man in a deep sleep, to give their desires their chance — which he handsomely admitted, for when a servant made bold to lay hands on some plate on the table, he cried out frankly, "What, you rogue? Don't you see that I am only sleeping for Maecenas?" There may be such, whose manners may be lewd enough but whose will is more upright than another's, who outwardly behaves more regularly. And we see some who complain of having vowed chastity before they knew what they did, and I have known others actually complain of having been given over to debauchery before they had reached the years of discretion. The vice of the parents, or the urge of nature — which is a rough counsellor — may be the cause.

In the East Indies, though chastity was held in singular reputation, custom permitted a married woman to prostitute herself to anyone who presented her with an elephant — and that to her glory, to have been valued at such a high price. Phaedo the philosopher, a man of birth, after the taking of his country, Elis, made it his trade to prostitute the beauty of his youth, so long as it lasted, to anyone who would pay him, in order to earn a living. And Solon was the first in Greece, it is said, to give women, by his laws, liberty to provide for the needs of life at the expense of their chastity — a custom that Herodotus says had been received in many states before his time. And anyway, what is the fruit of all this painful watching? For however just this passion may be, we still have to consider whether it gets us anywhere. Does anyone think to curb them, with all his ingenuity?
"Pone seram; cohibe: sed quis custodiet ipsos Custodes? cauta est, et ab illis incipit uxor."
["Put a lock on her; shut her up under a guard; but who shall guard the guards? Your wife is shrewd, and begins with them." — Juvenal, vi. 346.]
What kind of commodity will not serve their turn in such a knowing age?

Curiosity is vicious in general; but it is pernicious here. It is folly to investigate a disease for which there is no medicine that doesn't inflame and worsen it; whose shame grows still greater and more public through jealousy; and whose revenge wounds our children more than it heals us. You wither and die in the search for so obscure a proof. How miserably have those of my time arrived at such knowledge who have been unhappy enough to find it out! If the informer does not at the same time apply a remedy and bring relief, his information is harmful, and rather deserves a stab than a flat lie. We laugh as much at the man who labours to prevent it as at the man who is a cuckold and doesn't know it. The mark of cuckold is indelible; whoever once carries it carries it to his grave; the punishment proclaims it more than the fault. It is much to drag our private misfortunes out of obscurity and doubt, only to expose them on tragic scaffolds; misfortunes that hurt us only by being known. We say a woman is a good wife, or a marriage is happy, not because they really are so, but because no one says the contrary. Men should be wise enough to evade this tormenting and useless knowledge — and the Romans had a custom, when returning from any expedition, of sending home a messenger ahead to let their wives know of their coming, so they would not surprise them. And for this reason a certain nation has introduced the custom that on the wedding-day the priest shall open the way for the bride, to free the husband from the doubt and curiosity of examining, at the first assault, whether she comes a virgin to his bed or has been at the trade before.

But the world will be talking. I know a hundred honest men cuckolds, honestly and not unbecomingly. A worthy man is pitied for it, not held in less esteem. Order it so that your virtue overcomes your misfortune, that good men curse the occasion, and that he who wrongs you trembles only to think of it. Besides, who escapes being talked of in the same way, from the least to the greatest?
"Tot qui legionibus imperitivit Et melior quam to multis fuit, improbe, rebus."
["Many who have commanded legions, many a man much better than you, you rascal." — Lucretius, iii. 1039, 1041.]

Do you see how many honest men in your hearing are reproached with this? Then believe that you are no more spared elsewhere. But — even the ladies will laugh. And what are they so quick to laugh at in this virtuous age of ours as a peaceable and well-composed marriage? Each one of you has made somebody a cuckold; nature runs much in parallel, by compensation, turn for turn. The frequency of this accident ought long since to have made it more bearable; it has now passed into custom.
Miserable passion, which has this on top of everything else, that it cannot be shared:
"Fors etiam nostris invidit questibus aures;"
["Fortune itself refuses an ear to our complaints." — Catullus, lxvii.]

For to what friend dare you entrust your griefs, who, even if he doesn't laugh at them, won't make use of the occasion to get a share of the spoils? The bitterness, as well as the sweets, of marriage is kept secret by the wise; and among its other troublesome conditions, to a chatterer like me, this is one of the chief: that custom has made it indecent and prejudicial to communicate to anyone everything a man knows and feels. To give women the same counsel against jealousy would be so much time lost; their very being is so made up of suspicion, vanity, and curiosity that to cure them by any legitimate way is not to be hoped. They often recover from this infirmity by a kind of health more to be feared than the disease itself; for as there are enchantments which can only take away the evil by throwing it onto another, they will willingly transfer this one to their husbands when they shake it off themselves. And yet I do not know, to tell the truth, whether a man can suffer worse from them than their jealousy; it is the most dangerous of all their conditions, as the head is of all their members. Pittacus used to say that everyone had his trouble, and that his was his wife's jealous head; but for that, he would think himself perfectly happy. A mighty inconvenience, indeed, that could poison the whole life of so just, so wise, and so valiant a man — what must we lesser fellows do? The senate of Marseilles was right to grant his request to the man who begged leave to kill himself so he might be delivered from the clamour of his wife — for it is a misfortune that is never got rid of except by getting rid of the whole piece, and has no remedy but flight or patience, both of them very hard. It was, I think, an understanding man who said it was a happy marriage between a blind wife and a deaf husband.

Let us also consider whether the great and violent severity of obligation we impose on them does not produce two effects contrary to our design — that is, whether it does not make their pursuers more eager to attack, and the women more easy to yield. For as to the first, by raising the value of the place, we raise the value and desire of the conquest. Could it not be Venus herself who so cunningly raised the price of her merchandise by making the laws her procurers, knowing how flat a delight it would be that was not heightened by fancy and difficulty? In short, it is all pork, varied by sauces, as Flaminius' host said. Cupid is a roguish god who makes it his sport to contend with devotion and justice; it is his glory that his power outmatches all other powers, and that all other rules give place to his:
"Materiam culpae prosequiturque suae."
["And he seeks out a motive for his crimes." — Ovid, Trist., iv. 1. 34.]
As to the second point: should we not be less cuckolds if we less feared to be so — given the humour of women, whom prohibition incites and who are made more eager by being forbidden?
"Ubi velis, nolunt; ubi nolis, volunt ultro; Concessa pudet ire via."
["Where you want them to, they will not; where you do not want them to, they spontaneously agree; they are ashamed to go on the permitted road." — Terence, Eunuchus, act iv., sc. 8, v. 43.]

What better interpretation can we make of Messalina's behaviour? At first she made her husband a cuckold in private, as is the common practice; but, bringing her business about with too much ease, because of her husband's stupidity, she soon scorned that path and presently fell to making open love, to acknowledging her lovers, and to favouring and entertaining them in the sight of everyone. She wanted him to know it, to see it. The animal would not be roused by any of it, and made her pleasures dull and flat by his too-stupid acquiescence, by which he seemed to authorise and legitimate them — so what does she do? While she is the wife of a living and healthy emperor, in Rome, the theatre of the world, in the face of the sun and with solemn ceremony, she publicly marries Silius, who had long before enjoyed her, one day when her husband was out of town. Doesn't it look as if she meant to become chaste through her husband's negligence, or that she was looking for another husband who might sharpen her appetite by his jealousy, and incite her by watching her? But the first difficulty she met with was also the last; this beast was suddenly roused. These sleepy, sluggish men are often the most dangerous. I have found by experience that this extreme toleration, when it does dissolve, produces the most severe revenge: catching fire all at once, anger and fury combined into one, it discharges its utmost force at the first attack,
"Irarumque omnes effundit habenas:"
["He let loose all the reins of his fury." — Aeneid, xii. 499.]
he put her to death, along with a great number of those with whom she had had dealings, including even one who could not help himself, and whom she had had forced to her bed under the whip.
What Virgil says of Venus and Vulcan, Lucretius has expressed better, in a stolen enjoyment between Venus and Mars:

"Belli fera moenera Mavors Armipotens regit, ingremium qui saepe tuum se Rejictt, aeterno devinctus vulnere amoris ... Pascit amore avidos inhians in te, Dea, visus, Eque tuo pendet resupini spiritus ore Hunc tu, Diva, tuo recubantem corpore sancto Circumfusa super, suaveis ex ore loquelas Funde."

["Mars, the god of wars who controls the cruel labours of war, often reclines on your bosom, vanquished by the eternal wound of love, and there feeds his greedy gaze upon you, goddess, drinking love at his eyes; and as he lies back, his breath hangs upon your lips. Pour forth, divine one, sweet persuasive words, encircling him as he lies upon your sacred person." — Lucretius, i. 23.]

When I consider those words — rejicit, pascit, inhians, molli, fovet, medullas, labefacta, pendet, percurrit — and that splendid circumfusa, mother of the pretty infusus — I scorn those little quibbles and verbal allusions that have sprung up since. Those worthy men needed no subtlety to disguise their meaning; their language is downright, full of natural unbroken vigour. They are all epigram, not just the tail, but the head, body, and feet too. There is nothing forced, nothing languishing; everything keeps the same pace:
"Contextus totes virilis est; non sunt circa flosculos occupati."
["The whole texture is manly; they do not busy themselves about little flowers of rhetoric." — Seneca, Ep., 33.]

It is not a soft eloquence, and merely inoffensive; it is sinewy and solid, and does not so much please as fill and ravish the greatest minds. When I see these brave forms of expression, so lively, so deep, I do not say it is well said but well thought. It is the liveliness of the imagination that swells and lifts the words:
"Pectus est quod disertum Tacit."
["The heart is what makes a man eloquent." — Quintilian, x. 7.]

Our people call language, judgment, and fine words "full conceptions." This painting is done not so much by dexterity of hand as by having the object more vividly imprinted on the soul. Gallus speaks simply because he conceives simply.
